title: Verification and Iterative Improvement
summary: This intermediate module teaches a repeatable process for checking an AI-generated response against explicit requirements, revising identified problems, and verifying the revised result. After completing it, a learner can use recorded evidence and stopping conditions instead of relying on an overall impression of quality.
objectives: Translate a task into specific verification criteria.
Record a pass, fail, or unknown result for each criterion and support the result with evidence.
Revise a response to address identified failures without unnecessarily changing material that already passes.
Repeat verification after a revision and stop when every required criterion passes or any unresolved uncertainty is clearly disclosed.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The cited source changed. The prior repository-relative citation was associated with an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It has been replaced with a canonical arXiv record for research on iterative feedback and refinement.

The change affects source provenance and the support for the explanation of iterative refinement. The verification workflow itself remains unchanged. The cited research reports results for the method and evaluations described in that paper; it does not establish that every revision process will improve every response.

sections.title: Intermediate-level foundation
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can read a generated response, identify the requirements in a task, and make a basic textual revision. It does not assume experience with a named provider, programming interface, or evaluation framework.

Verification is a deliberate comparison between a candidate response and explicit criteria. Revision is the act of changing the candidate after verification identifies a failure, unsupported claim, or unresolved uncertainty. Keeping these activities distinct makes it possible to explain why each change was made.

sections.title: Define verifiable criteria
paragraphs: Begin by translating the task into criteria that can be checked separately. A useful criterion identifies an observable property, such as the presence of a required field, the use of an allowed value, support for a factual statement, or compliance with a requested format.

Avoid a criterion such as "make it good" because it does not define what evidence would count as success. Replace it with concrete checks appropriate to the task, such as "every factual claim has an accessible source" or "the response contains exactly one object and no surrounding text."

Preserve the distinction between required criteria and optional preferences. A response fails when it violates a requirement. An unmet preference may justify improvement, but it should not be mislabeled as a failure unless the task made it mandatory.

sections.title: Record verification evidence
paragraphs: Check each criterion independently and record one of three outcomes: pass, fail, or unknown. Mark pass only when the response contains evidence that satisfies the criterion. Mark fail when available evidence shows that it does not. Mark unknown when the necessary evidence is unavailable.

Evidence should be specific enough for another reviewer to repeat the check. Depending on the criterion, evidence might be an exact passage, a field and its value, a calculation, or a resolvable source that supports a factual claim.

Do not convert unknown into pass. Seek the missing evidence when possible. If the uncertainty cannot be resolved, omit the unsupported claim or disclose the unresolved limitation, according to the task's requirements.
sections.callout: A confident tone is not verification evidence.

sections.title: Revise only what the evidence identifies
paragraphs: Use the verification record to choose revisions. For each failed criterion, identify the smallest change that can correct the failure. For an unknown result, first determine whether additional evidence can resolve it. If not, remove the unsupported assertion rather than replacing uncertainty with a guess.

Leave passing material alone unless a required correction depends on changing it. Controlled revisions preserve reviewed work and make it easier to see whether the change addressed the recorded problem.

Iterative feedback and refinement have been studied as a way to improve generated responses. The cited paper describes a process in which a model produces feedback on an output and then refines that output repeatedly. Its reported findings support teaching iteration as a useful technique within the studied setting, not as a guarantee of universal improvement.

sections.title: Verify again and apply a stopping condition
paragraphs: After revising, run the complete set of criteria again rather than checking only the item that previously failed. A change that fixes one problem can introduce another, so earlier passing results must be confirmed against the revised candidate.

Stop when every required criterion passes. If a required fact remains unknown and the task permits disclosure, stop only after clearly identifying that limitation. If the task does not permit unresolved required information, the candidate is not ready.

The completed record should connect each requirement to an outcome, the evidence for that outcome, and any revision made in response. After this module, you can create and use that record to guide a response from an initial candidate to a verified result.

questions.prompt: Which criterion is most directly verifiable?
choices: Every factual claim has an accessible supporting source.
questions.explanation: The source requirement identifies an observable property that can be checked for each factual claim. The other choices rely on undefined overall judgments.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer record when the evidence needed to evaluate a criterion is unavailable?
questions.explanation: The module defines unknown as the outcome used when the evidence needed for a pass or fail decision is unavailable.

questions.prompt: What is the preferred scope of a revision after verification identifies one failed criterion?
choices: Change the smallest amount needed to correct the failure and leave passing material alone.
Remove all criteria from the verification record.
Treat the failed criterion as optional.
questions.explanation: Controlled revision addresses the recorded failure while preserving material that already passes.

questions.prompt: What should happen immediately after a candidate has been revised?
choices: Check only the sentence that changed.
Run the complete set of verification criteria again.
Replace all pass results with unknown.
questions.explanation: The module requires checking the complete criteria set again because a revision can affect requirements that previously passed.

activity.title: Verification and Iterative Improvement Practical Lab
instructions: Review the scenario requirements and parameters.
Execute the practical steps in your development environment.
Validate the output traces against the expected assertions.
Document conclusions and submit the result.
